title: Briefcase is an Agentic AI portfolio manager, it can’t directly give financial advice due to laws but can do everything else
author: Emojinapp
selftext:
I originally called Briefcase a “news stock agent” while building it because news is actually a core part of how its AI works.

You add your portfolio, including stocks, bonds, crypto, cash, and physical assets, and Briefcase continuously connects what you own with relevant news headlines. Its agentic pipeline uses those headlines as context and verification before generating insights about what may be affecting your holdings.

So instead of asking an LLM a generic question about a stock, the agent starts with two things it knows: **what you actually own and what is happening around those assets right now.** It can then connect a headline to a holding, explain why it may be relevant, and surface changes across the broader portfolio.

It deliberately stops short of telling you what to buy or sell. The goal is to handle everything around that decision better: monitoring the portfolio, finding relevant news, cross-referencing it against your holdings, and turning that information into useful context.

Briefcase has recently started getting App Store downloads without me actively promoting it, so I figured I should actually start talking about what the agent does.

Would love to hear what people here would want a portfolio/news agent like this to handle next.

App Store: [https://apps.apple.com/us/app/briefcase-ai-portfolio/id6758148658](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/briefcase-ai-portfolio/id6758148658)

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The piece I would want handled next is attribution. Connecting a headline to a holding is the easy part and most of the time it is wrong, in the sense that the thing moved for reasons nobody wrote about that morning. Put a headline next to a move and you imply a cause the pipeline cannot actually establish.

Showing how often a flagged headline was followed by nothing would make everything else in there easier to trust.

replies.author: Emojinapp
replies.body: Oh it does that already, it tells you when a move is unexplained, the news is just one of the input sources of the agentic pipeline. The frontier model is also hardened against clickbait and prompt injection. You also have a chat mode where you can freely query the agent in any direction you choose

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: hardened against prompt injection is a big claim for something whose job is ingesting news. what does it do when a headline carries instructions and the underlying move is real?

replies.author: Emojinapp
replies.body: I treat the instruction as untrusted information and then look for additional sources that can either verify or refute it, the last update, injection hardening was the aspect I worked on the most. I ran thorough pen tests with fable and Astra and the agent rejected all their injection attempts. For something used in financial research we have to mitigate such risks

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Two models failing to break it is a floor, not a ceiling. Both are trying the attacks they already know. The one that gets you arrives inside a document the agent was asked to summarise, not in a prompt aimed at it.

replies.author: Emojinapp
replies.body: Fable has been known to find day 1 bugs in apps that have existed for decades so the kinds of exploits it writes are superior to one a human hacker can. Also the agentic pen testing was just the final step. We ran over 100 untrusted articles and the agent handled them very well, showing clear disclaimers for baseless claims and sensational reporting and letting us know when a claim has legs from multiple verifiable sources. Revealing my entire system would simply make it less secure, but I’m quite confident the bar was set high enough. We expect prompt injections to come from every angle I and we block them at the root, even the user themselves can prompt inject the agent to make it state an unverifiable claim as truth

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Passing a hundred from one generator mostly tells you about that generator. The injections that land in the wild are usually boring rather than clever, and they arrive inside content the user actually asked for. Do you replay the ones that got through early back in as a regression set?

replies.author: Emojinapp
replies.body: Why would you think I won’t account for every kind of injection? The obvious ones are just the basic layer, I account for subtle and complex injections alike. The gates are layered

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: I wasn't doubting the layers, I meant the denominator. 100 articles that mostly contain no attack tells you the false positive rate and not much about the catch rate. the number I'd want is how many of those 100 were actually hostile.

replies.author: Emojinapp
replies.body: lol I went for low reputation articles because they are the ones with the injection attempts, you don’t expect cnn or Bloomberg to publish prompt injection baits. And I didn’t say it didn’t catch any injections, it caught a lot of them, that was the standard we used for our automated tests afterwards. More than 70% of the 100 were flagged as sensational and ungrounded

replies.author: mojovski
replies.body: Don't worry. It's all ai slop.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Grounding the agent in what you actually own before it touches any news feed is the right sequencing, most 'AI stock news' tools do it backwards: they summarize headlines first and then try to guess relevance to a portfolio after the fact, which is where a lot of noise creeps in. Stopping short of buy/sell is smart both legally and practically, the connective tissue between a headline and a holding is genuinely the hard, valuable part, the recommendation itself is the easy part everyone already has opinions about. One thing worth probing as you get more users: how are you handling relevance decay, a headline that mattered the day it dropped often stops being useful within 24-48 hours, so surfacing it as 'still relevant' a week later erodes trust fast even if the connection was technically accurate. Also curious whether you're doing this per-asset or trying to catch second-order effects too (e.g. a supplier's earnings miss affecting a holding indirectly), since that's a much harder but more valuable problem than direct headline-to-ticker matching.

Similar problem space to what I'm building with EventTrader, though I'm coming at it more from the event-driven signal side than portfolio-news correlation, always good to see how other people are drawing the line on what the agent should and shouldn't decide for the user. [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)
